parole.testo: Probably first used in the aristocratic Persian of the Mughal empire, from at least the 1650s. The word spread from South Asia to the rest of the Persianate world. The first attestation by an author of Iranian origin is apparently from Tohfat al-'âlam (1801), itself a memoir of the author's journeys

A Wanderwort, probably from northwestern Indo-Aryan: compare Punjabi ਟੱਬਰ (ṭabbar, “extended family”), Urdu ٹَبَّر (ṭabbar, “extended family”, borrowed from Punjabi), and Pashto ټبر (ṭabə́r, “tribe, clan, people”). Note that the Pashto is clearly borrowed from Indo-Aryan, given the presence of retro
An Indo-Aryan borrowing, ultimately from Sanskrit यन्त्र (yantra).

Borrowed from an Indo-Aryan language. Compare Hindi दुशाला (duśālā), from Sanskrit शाटी (śāṭī), feminine of शाट (śāṭa, “clothing”). Sometimes said to be from or influenced by Chāliāt, a Persian pronunciation of Chaliyam in India, supposedly where they were first made. Doublet of سَارِی (sārī /sâri).
An Indo-Aryan borrowing, ultimately from Sanskrit माम (māma), itself from Proto-Dravidian *māma. Akin to Pashto, Baluchi, and Urdu ماما (māmā), Hindi मामा (māmā).
An Indo-Aryan borrowing. Perhaps borrowed from Hindustani पट्टू (paṭṭū, “coarse woollen cloth”). Compare Hindi पट (paṭ, “garment, cloth”), Sanskrit पट्ट (paṭṭa, “cloth, garment”).
Likely borrowed from a Indo-Aryan language; probably from Hindustani (see Hindi काँच (kā̃c) / Urdu کان٘چ (kā̃c)), ultimately from Sanskrit काच (kāca).

An Indo-Aryan borrowing, ultimately from Proto-Middle Indo-Aryan *𑀓𑀸𑀓𑁆𑀓 (*kākka), itself a Dravidian borrowing. Likely via Hindustani काका / کاکا (kākā). Akin to Baluchi کاکا and Pashto کاکا (kākā). All meaning paternal uncle or an older male.

Borrowed from Indo-Aryan (compare Sanskrit कोटपाल/कोट्टपाल (koṭapāla/koṭṭapāla), Urdu کٹھوال (kṭhvāl), Hindi कोतवाल (kotvāl, “police chief”)) or Turkic (compare Chagatai کوتاوال (kwtʾwʾl) / کوتاول (kwtʾwl)). Attested since the Ghaznavid period.
